items.title: Your liver and your eyes have separate clocks
items.claim: Every cell in your body has its own molecular clock. The 'master' clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronises them. Eating at the wrong time can desynchronise organs from each other — same as jet lag without the travel.
items.prompt: What is a cellular circadian clock made of?

options.text: A transcription-translation feedback loop: genes (BMAL1/CLOCK in mammals) drive expression of inhibitor proteins (PER, CRY) that themselves repress the original genes — the cycle takes about 24 hours to complete
An internal sundial of pigment molecules

items.reveal:
In Drosophila, Hall, Rosbash and Young identified Period (PER) gene and worked out the negative feedback loop: PER protein accumulates in the cell, eventually shuts down its own transcription, then degrades, allowing the cycle to repeat. Mammals have BMAL1/CLOCK driving PER1/2/3 and CRY1/2, with the same logic.

The cycle's intrinsic period is close to 24 hours; light input (via melanopsin in retinal ganglion cells) synchronises it to the day.

Peripheral clocks (in liver, muscle, fat) entrain primarily to feeding times. Eating at midnight tells your liver it's daytime even as your SCN says it's night — exactly the desynchronisation seen in shift workers, who have elevated rates of metabolic disease and some cancers.
items.why: The biological clock is pictured as one master organ. Every cell has one, and keeping them aligned is a daily ongoing process — and easily disrupted.

items.title: PCR exists because of a bacterium living in a hot spring
items.claim: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) cycles between ~95 C (denature DNA) and ~60 C (anneal primers). Most enzymes would be cooked. PCR works because Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus (Yellowstone hot springs), has a stable structure at boiling temperatures.

options.text: Polymerase from any organism could work

Without a heat-stable polymerase, every PCR cycle would require fresh enzyme — impractical. Taq DNA polymerase survives 95 C and made automated PCR feasible (Mullis 1985, Nobel 1993), transforming molecular biology, forensics and medical diagnosis
Yellowstone bacteria are specially treated for use
PCR doesn't really need hot temperatures

items.reveal:
Thomas Brock isolated Thermus aquaticus from hot springs at Yellowstone in 1969, purely out of curiosity. He showed bacteria thrive at temperatures up to 80 C — far hotter than was thought possible at the time.

Fifteen years later, Kary Mullis (Cetus Corporation) invents PCR. The first version uses E. coli DNA polymerase — denatured each cycle, requiring fresh enzyme to be added every 30 seconds for 30+ cycles. Tedious.

Taq DNA polymerase, isolated from T. aquaticus, survives the high temperatures. PCR becomes automatable. The PCR machine — a programmable thermocycler — becomes a standard piece of every molecular lab.

PCR transformed:
- Molecular cloning (you can amplify any DNA without growing it in bacteria first).
- Genetic testing and diagnosis.
- Forensics (DNA fingerprinting from tiny samples).
- Genome sequencing (most methods start with PCR amplification).
- Real-time PCR for COVID-19 diagnosis during the pandemic.

Other extremophile biotech:
- Vent polymerases (from hydrothermal vents) for higher-fidelity PCR.
- Detergent enzymes (proteases, lipases) from psychrophilic bacteria work at low temperatures, allowing cold-water washing.
- DNA-melting and structure-determining enzymes from various thermophiles.

Basic research on 'irrelevant' bacteria led to a transformative technology.
items.why: PCR seems like an obvious technique. It required a bacterium that no one had a use for, found in a place no one expected life to be. Basic, curiosity-driven biology paid off enormously.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.
